title: The Generations of Esau, Who Is Edom
summary: Genesis 36 records Esau’s wives, sons, chiefs, and kings, showing God keeping his word to Esau while the line of promise waits in Canaan.
historicalContext: Edom occupied the rugged highlands of Seir east and south of the Dead Sea, a plateau of red sandstone cut by deep ravines and bounded on the north by the brook Zered and on the west by the Arabah rift. Before Esau’s family arrived, Horite clans held the region (14:6), and the descendants of Esau either absorbed them by marriage or drove them out (Deuteronomy 2:12, 22). Egyptian frontier records from the later second millennium before Christ speak of herding clans from Seir and Edom, which fits the picture of tribal chiefs given here. Edom had a king when Moses asked leave to pass through its land (Numbers 20:14-21). Saul fought Edom, David garrisoned it, and the two peoples remained rivals through the prophets. In later centuries the Edomites, called Idumeans, were forcibly joined to Judea, and from them came the Herods who ruled in Jesus’ day.
literaryContext: The chapter carries the ninth “generations” heading of Genesis (36:1), repeated in verse 9 as Esau’s household grows into a nation. As Ishmael’s line (25:12-18) was recorded before the story of Isaac’s sons, Esau’s line is set down before the story of Jacob’s family begins (37:2). The material falls into five blocks: Esau’s family in Canaan and his move to Seir (vv. 1-8), his sons and the chiefs descended from them (vv. 9-19), the Horite clans of Seir (vv. 20-30), eight kings of Edom (vv. 31-39), and a closing roll of chiefs by their districts (vv. 40-43). The refrain “Esau is Edom” (vv. 1, 8, 19, 43) binds the lists together. Immediately afterward, “Jacob dwelt in the land wherein his father was a stranger” (37:1) sets the settled, powerful Esau beside the waiting heir of the promise.
themes: God’s faithfulness to the brother outside the chosen line
Separation of the two brothers and their lands
Earthly greatness that arrives before the promise
Edom’s clans, chiefs, and kings as a nation formed
The land of promise kept for Jacob’s seed
A remnant of Edom foreseen among the gathered nations

outline.title: Esau’s Family and His Move to Seir
outline.summary: Esau’s three wives and five sons born in Canaan are named, and he leaves the land of Canaan for mount Seir because the brothers’ herds are too large to share it.

outline.title: The Sons and Chiefs of Esau
outline.summary: Esau’s sons and grandsons are listed by their mothers and then ranked as the dukes who led the clans of Edom.

outline.title: The Horites of Seir
outline.summary: The earlier inhabitants of the land, the sons of Seir the Horite, are listed with their children and chiefs, including the women who joined their line to Esau’s.

outline.title: The Kings of Edom
outline.summary: Eight kings, none succeeded by his son, reign in Edom before any king rules over Israel.

outline.title: The Chiefs of Edom by Their Places
outline.summary: Eleven chiefs are named according to their families and districts, and the chapter closes by naming Esau the father of the Edomites.

verses.bibleText: Now these are the generations of Esau, who is Edom.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Now these are the generations of Esau” opens a new section of Genesis, and its placement is telling. Isaac has just been buried by both of his sons (35:29). Before the story turns to Jacob’s family and Joseph, Genesis gives an account of the brother who will not carry the promise, just as Ishmael’s family was recorded (25:12-18) before the history of Isaac’s sons began (25:19). The book handles the side branch first and then returns to the chosen line. Esau is set aside from the covenant line, yet he is not forgotten; his family receives the longest genealogy given to any non-chosen line in the book.

“Who is Edom” connects the man with the nation. Esau was born “red, all over like an hairy garment” (25:25), and he gained the name Edom when he begged for the “red pottage” and sold his birthright for it (25:30-34). The clarifying phrase recurs four times in the chapter (vv. 1, 8, 19, 43) like a refrain. The appetite of one afternoon became the name of a people, and Hebrews holds up that exchange as a warning against treating holy things lightly (Hebrews 12:16-17).

The chapter is also a record of God’s faithfulness. Before the twins were born, the LORD told Rebekah, “Two nations are in thy womb” (25:23). Isaac, speaking “by faith” (Hebrews 11:20), promised Esau a dwelling with “the fatness of the earth” and a life by the sword (27:39-40). Every name that follows shows those words coming true. If God keeps the secondary promises made to Esau so thoroughly, then the greater promises carried by Jacob’s line are secure.

Edom’s later history was often bitter, yet the prophets did not leave it there. Amos foresaw “the remnant of Edom” among the nations called by the LORD’s name (Amos 9:12), and James applied that prophecy to Gentiles entering the people of Christ (Acts 15:16-17). The generations of Esau stand within the same purpose that will one day gather Jacob’s estranged brother.

wordNotes.explanation: The name sounds like the adjective ʾadom, “red,” the word Esau used when he demanded the “red pottage,” and it echoes his ruddy appearance at birth (ʾadmoni). Genesis connects the national name with both moments. Later Scripture uses Edom both for Esau’s descendants and for their territory in Seir, and Moses addresses Edom’s king as “thy brother Israel.”

wordNotes.term: אֵלֶּה תֹּלְדוֹת עֵשָׂו (ʾelleh toledot ʿEsav) — these are the generations of Esau
wordNotes.explanation: The heading formula marks the ninth major section of Genesis. Only here is the same heading given twice for one man (36:1, 9): the first introduces Esau’s household in Canaan, and the second introduces Esau as the father of a nation in Seir. The pattern of recording the non-chosen son before the chosen one follows Ishmael and Isaac.

verses.bibleText: Esau took his wives of the daughters of Canaan; Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Aholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Esau took his wives of the daughters of Canaan” recalls an old wound. His Hittite marriages were “a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah” (26:34-35), and Rebekah used them to justify sending Jacob away to find a wife among their own kin (27:46; 28:1). Abraham had insisted that Isaac not marry a Canaanite (24:3). Esau ignored that pattern, and the phrase placed at the head of his family history shows that he joined his house to the peoples whose land God had promised to Abraham’s seed.

Adah is the daughter of Elon the Hittite. Aholibamah is “the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite,” and she reappears in the Horite list (vv. 24-25), so “Hivite” here likely describes her family loosely, or reflects a scribal slip; the Greek translation reads “Horite.”

The names differ from the earlier lists, which name Judith, Bashemath the daughter of Elon, and Mahalath (26:34; 28:9). People in the ancient world often bore more than one name, and women frequently received a new name at marriage. Adah may be the Bashemath of 26:34, while Judith may have died childless and been replaced by Aholibamah. Genealogies normally list the wives who bore sons, which explains why the roster changes.

wordNotes.explanation: The name appears to combine ʾohel, “tent,” with bamah, “high place,” possibly meaning “tent of the high place.” A high place was an elevated shrine, and later Scripture associates such sites with Canaanite worship. Personal names did not always carry their literal sense in daily use, but this one suits the Canaanite setting of Esau’s marriages. The same name later designates an Edomite clan.

verses.bibleText: And Bashemath Ishmael's daughter, sister of Nebajoth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Bashemath, “Ishmael’s daughter, sister of Nebajoth,” is the wife called Mahalath in 28:9. Esau married her after he saw that “the daughters of Canaan pleased not Isaac his father” (28:8). It was an attempt to win approval by marrying into Abraham’s family, but he chose the branch Abraham had already sent away (21:10-14). The two non-chosen lines, Ishmael’s and Esau’s, were joined in this marriage.

Nebajoth was Ishmael’s firstborn (25:13), and his people became known for their flocks. Isaiah pictures “the rams of Nebaioth” offered on God’s altar when the nations stream to Zion (Isaiah 60:7). The family Esau married into would one day be pictured bringing worship to the house of God.

wordNotes.explanation: The name is related to besem, “spice” or “balsam,” and suggests fragrance. It was evidently a favored name; Esau had two wives called by it at different times (26:34; 36:3), and Solomon later gave it to one of his daughters. The spice word appears among the fragrant ingredients of the holy anointing oil.

verses.bibleText: And Adah bare to Esau Eliphaz; and Bashemath bare Reuel;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Adah bore Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn, and Bashemath bore Reuel. Both names contain El, the Hebrew word for God. Eliphaz may mean “God is fine gold” or “my God is strength,” and Reuel means “friend of God.” Such names suggest that the memory of the God of Abraham and Isaac lingered in Esau’s household, even though his marriages pulled it toward the peoples of Canaan.

Each name surfaces again in Scripture. Job’s first counselor was “Eliphaz the Temanite” (Job 2:11), and since Teman was the eldest son of this Eliphaz (v. 11), Job’s friend likely belonged to the Edomite clan descended from him. Reuel was also the name of Moses’ father-in-law, the priest of Midian (Exodus 2:18). Edom’s wisdom tradition, which Jeremiah later mourned (Jeremiah 49:7), may have grown from these early roots.

wordNotes.explanation: The name joins reaʿ, “friend” or “companion,” with ʾEl, “God,” and so means “friend of God.” It was borne by Esau’s son, by Moses’ Midianite father-in-law (also called Raguel), and by a man of Gad. Its spread across several peoples shows how widely the name of God was still invoked in the patriarchal world.

verses.bibleText: And Aholibamah bare Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah: these are the sons of Esau, which were born unto him in the land of Canaan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Aholibamah bore three sons: Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah. Jeush may mean “he will help,” Jaalam perhaps relates to the mountain goat, and Korah means “bald.” The name Korah later belonged to the Levite who rebelled against Moses (Numbers 16:1); yet “the children of Korah died not” (Numbers 26:11), and his descendants became temple singers whose names stand over several psalms.

The closing note matters: “these are the sons of Esau, which were born unto him in the land of Canaan.” Jacob’s sons, except Benjamin, were born in Paddan-aram (35:26), far from the land, yet they would inherit it. Esau’s sons were born in Canaan, yet they would leave it. Birth in the land did not make anyone an heir of the promise, as Paul observed: “neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children” (Romans 9:7).

wordNotes.explanation: The name is often linked to a verb meaning to help or come to aid, giving the sense “he helps” or “may he help.” It later appears among the Benjamites, the Levites, and the sons of King Rehoboam, showing that names shared by Israel and Edom reflect a common heritage.

verses.bibleText: And Esau took his wives, and his sons, and his daughters, and all the persons of his house, and his cattle, and all his beasts, and all his substance, which he had got in the land of Canaan; and went into the country from the face of his brother Jacob.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The verse lists everything Esau took: “his wives, and his sons, and his daughters, and all the persons of his house, and his cattle, and all his beasts, and all his substance.” The inventory is complete. Nothing remains behind to tie Esau to Canaan, and the phrase “which he had got in the land of Canaan” reminds the reader that his wealth was gathered there. The fatness of the earth that Isaac had spoken over him (27:39) was real, and he carried it away.

Esau had already gained a foothold in Seir before Jacob returned from Haran; Jacob sent messengers “unto Esau his brother unto the land of Seir” (32:3), and Esau went back there after their meeting (33:16). This verse records the final, complete move of the household. The KJV’s “into the country” renders a Hebrew phrase that names no land; verse 8 supplies the destination.

The wording recalls Abram and Lot. When their herds could no longer share the land, Lot “chose him all the plain of Jordan” and moved toward Sodom (13:11). Esau, too, moved away from the land of promise toward a territory he could hold at once. Yet the move was no theft. Moses later reminded Israel that God himself had given “mount Seir unto Esau for a possession” and forbade them to take even a foot of it (Deuteronomy 2:5; Joshua 24:4). The separation was peaceful, the reconciliation of chapter 33 held, and the brothers had just stood together at their father’s grave.

The contrast still speaks. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob “sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country” because they looked for a city whose builder is God (Hebrews 11:9-10). Esau settled for a portion he could see. Those who belong to Christ are called to the patriarchs’ kind of patience.

wordNotes.term: מִפְּנֵי יַעֲקֹב אָחִיו (mippene Yaʿaqov ʾaḥiv) — from the face of his brother Jacob
wordNotes.explanation: The compound preposition mippene, literally “from the face of,” can express fleeing from someone or simply moving away from their presence. Earlier Jacob “fled from the face of Esau” (35:1, 7). Now the movement is reversed: Esau leaves the presence of Jacob. Here the phrase describes separation without hostility, since the brothers had been reconciled.

The noun denotes movable property, especially livestock and goods acquired over time. Genesis uses it for Abram’s possessions when he entered Canaan, for the wealth that forced Abram and Lot apart, and for what Jacob brought back from Paddan-aram. Each time it marks God’s material blessing, which can either serve the promise or draw a person away from it.

verses.bibleText: For their riches were more than that they might dwell together; and the land wherein they were strangers could not bear them because of their cattle.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For their riches were more than that they might dwell together” gives the reason for the move, and it nearly repeats the words used of Abram and Lot: “the land was not able to bear them … for their substance was great” (13:6). Both brothers had been blessed. Jacob returned from Haran with “much cattle, and maidservants, and menservants, and camels, and asses” (30:43), and Esau met him with four hundred men (32:6). Unlike the earlier separation, no quarrel between herdsmen is mentioned. Prosperity made the parting necessary, and it seems to have been arranged in peace.

“The land wherein they were strangers” is a striking description of Canaan. Even after three generations, the patriarchs owned no land there except a burial cave bought from Ephron (23:17-20). God had promised the land “for an everlasting possession” (17:8), but Isaac’s sons still lived in it as resident aliens. The promise of ownership lay in the future.

That situation tested each brother’s hope. Esau went where he could own land at once. Jacob remained where he had only a promise. Hebrews describes the patriarchs as having died “not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off,” confessing that “they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13). Jacob’s choice to stay belongs to that confession.

wordNotes.term: אֶרֶץ מְגוּרֵיהֶם (ʾerets megurehem) — the land wherein they were strangers
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the land of their sojournings,” from gur, “to live as a resident alien.” God promised Abraham and Jacob “the land wherein thou art a stranger,” and the very next verse after this chapter says Jacob dwelt in “the land wherein his father was a stranger.” The phrase holds together present homelessness and future inheritance.

verses.bibleText: Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir: Esau is Edom.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir” closes the first section. Seir is the high, broken country running south from the brook Zered toward the Gulf of Aqaba, east of the Arabah rift. Its red sandstone cliffs and narrow gorges made it a natural fortress, and the prophets later spoke of Edom’s pride in nesting “in the clefts of the rock” and setting its nest “among the stars” (Obadiah 1:3-4; Jeremiah 49:16). Horite clans had lived there long before Esau arrived (14:6; v. 20).

The name Seir sounds like seʿar, “hair,” the very word used of Esau at birth when he came out “like an hairy garment” (25:25). The hairy man settled in the shaggy, wooded hills that shared his description. “Esau is Edom” again joins the person to the nation that would bear his story.

The verb “dwelt” prepares a contrast that comes two verses after the chapter ends: “And Jacob dwelt in the land wherein his father was a stranger” (37:1). Each brother settled, but in different lands and on different terms. God honored Esau’s portion; he told Israel, “I have given mount Seir unto Esau for a possession” (Deuteronomy 2:5).

The mountain did not have the last word. Balaam foresaw that “Seir also shall be a possession for his enemies” when a Star rises out of Jacob (Numbers 24:17-18), and Obadiah closed his prophecy with saviours on mount Zion judging “the mount of Esau,” ending with the declaration, “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s” (Obadiah 1:21). The two mountains point to the reign of Christ, which will gather the redeemed of every nation.

wordNotes.explanation: Har can mean a single mountain or a mountainous region; here it denotes the whole highland of Edom. The name Seir resembles seʿar, “hair,” perhaps describing rough, scrub-covered slopes, and Genesis plays on the resemblance to Esau’s hairy appearance. Ezekiel addresses the region directly in an oracle against Edom’s hatred of Israel.

The verb yashav means to sit, settle, or remain. Genesis uses the same form for Esau settling in Seir and for Jacob dwelling in Canaan (37:1), creating a deliberate pair. Lot, too, “dwelled in the cities of the plain” after separating from Abram, and the comparison is instructive.

verses.bibleText: And these are the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in mount Seir:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The heading “these are the generations of Esau” is repeated, but with a new description: “Esau the father of the Edomites in mount Seir.” Verse 1 introduced a man and his household in Canaan; verse 9 introduces the founder of a nation settled in its own territory. What follows restates the sons already named and then adds the grandsons whose families became the clans of Edom.

Moses would later instruct Israel to pass by “your brethren the children of Esau, which dwell in Seir” with care, paying for food and water (Deuteronomy 2:4-6). The word “brethren” keeps the family bond in view. The parallel record in 1 Chronicles 1:35-37 shows that Israel preserved this list for centuries.

wordNotes.term: אֲבִי אֱדוֹם (ʾavi ʾEdom) — the father of the Edomites
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the father of Edom.” In Hebrew genealogy “father” often means founder or ancestor of a people or a town. God renamed Abram “a father of many nations,” and Lot’s sons are called the fathers of the Moabites and Ammonites. Esau is presented here as the head of a whole national family.

verses.bibleText: These are the names of Esau's sons; Eliphaz the son of Adah the wife of Esau, Reuel the son of Bashemath the wife of Esau.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Only two of Esau’s five sons are named here, Eliphaz the son of Adah and Reuel the son of Bashemath, because their own sons founded the clans that follow. Aholibamah’s three sons are taken up separately in verse 14, since they themselves became chiefs.

Each son is identified by his mother, just as Jacob’s sons were grouped by Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah (35:23-26). In a household with several wives, a son’s standing depended on his mother, and the arrangement kept the lines distinct. Jacob’s home showed how such households could breed rivalry (30:1); Esau’s list simply records the order.

wordNotes.term: אֵשֶׁת עֵשָׂו (ʾeshet ʿEsav) — the wife of Esau
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase is repeated for Adah, Bashemath, and Aholibamah throughout verses 10-18. It marks each as a full wife, in contrast with Timna, the concubine of Eliphaz (v. 12). Genesis draws the same distinction elsewhere, as when Sarai gave Hagar to Abram “to be his wife” and when Rachel gave Bilhah to Jacob.

verses.bibleText: And the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Eliphaz’s five sons were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz. Teman, meaning “south,” gave his name to an important district of Edom and sometimes to the whole nation. Jeremiah asked, “Is wisdom no more in Teman?” (Jeremiah 49:7), Amos foretold fire on Teman (Amos 1:12), and Habakkuk saw God coming “from Teman” in his vision of the LORD marching from the south (Habakkuk 3:3). Job’s friend Eliphaz the Temanite likely came from this clan.

Omar, Zepho (Zephi in 1 Chronicles 1:36), and Gatam appear nowhere else. Kenaz is more intriguing. The Kenizzites appear among the peoples of Canaan (15:19), and Caleb is called “the Kenezite” (Numbers 32:12), while his younger kinsman Othniel is “the son of Kenaz” (Judges 1:13). This suggests that a clan of Edomite origin was absorbed into Judah. One of Israel’s most faithful men, who “wholly followed the LORD,” may have come from Esau’s family by way of that clan.

wordNotes.explanation: The word means “south” or “right side,” since a person facing east has the south on the right hand. As a proper name it denotes a clan and district of Edom, renowned for wisdom and later threatened with judgment. In Habakkuk’s psalm, God’s appearing from Teman recalls his coming to Israel from the southern wilderness.

The same name is borne by the ancestor of the Kenizzites, by Caleb’s family, and by Othniel’s father. Caleb is called both a Kenezite and a leader of Judah, suggesting that an outside clan joined Israel and became fully part of it. Caleb’s wholehearted faith shows that grafted-in families could stand among the most faithful in Israel.

verses.bibleText: And Timna was concubine to Eliphaz Esau's son; and she bare to Eliphaz Amalek: these were the sons of Adah Esau's wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Timna, the concubine of Eliphaz, was the sister of Lotan the Horite (v. 22). The marriage shows Esau’s family intertwining with the native ruling families of Seir, a step toward taking over their land. Timna bore Amalek, and the verse counts him among “the sons of Adah,” since he was Adah’s grandson. The shorter list in 1 Chronicles 1:36 compresses the line and places Timna and Amalek directly after Eliphaz’s sons.

Amalek became the ancestor of Israel’s fiercest desert enemy. The Amalekites were the first to attack Israel after the exodus, at Rephidim, where Israel prevailed while Moses’ hands were held up toward heaven (Exodus 17:8-16). Moses later recalled that they struck “all that were feeble behind” when Israel was “faint and weary,” and that they “feared not God” (Deuteronomy 25:17-18). Balaam called Amalek “the first of the nations” (Numbers 24:20), the first to oppose God’s people on their way to the land.

The conflict ran through Israel’s history. Saul lost his kingdom partly because he spared the Amalekite king Agag (1 Samuel 15), and a remnant of Amalek was finally destroyed in Hezekiah’s day (1 Chronicles 4:42-43). The mention of “the country of the Amalekites” in Abraham’s time (14:7) uses the later name for the region. A single line about a concubine’s son introduces a people whose hostility tested Israel’s reliance on God for generations.

wordNotes.explanation: A concubine was a secondary wife, legally bound to her husband but without the full standing of a primary wife. Her children could be treated differently in matters of inheritance, as Abraham sent the sons of his concubines away with gifts. Bilhah, too, is called Jacob’s concubine.

The name designates both Esau’s grandson and the nomadic people descended from him, who ranged through the Negeb and the Sinai. God commanded that the memory of Amalek be blotted out because of its unprovoked cruelty toward Israel, a judgment later entrusted to Saul.

verses.bibleText: And these are the sons of Reuel; Nahath, and Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah: these were the sons of Bashemath Esau's wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Reuel’s four sons were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. Several of these names also appear in Israel. Zerah was the name of one of Judah’s twin sons (38:30), and a king of Edom is later called “Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah” (v. 33), perhaps from this clan. Shammah was the name of David’s brother (1 Samuel 16:9) and of one of David’s mighty men (2 Samuel 23:11). Nahath occurs among the Levites (1 Chronicles 6:26).

Mizzah is otherwise unknown. The overlap in names reflects the shared language and ancestry of the two brother nations, whose kinship Scripture never lets Israel forget.

wordNotes.explanation: The name comes from zaraḥ, “to rise” or “shine,” used of the sun coming up. Isaiah speaks of nations coming “to the brightness of thy rising,” and Malachi promises that “the Sun of righteousness” shall “arise with healing in his wings,” using the same verb for the coming of the Messiah.

verses.bibleText: And these were the sons of Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: and she bare to Esau Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Aholibamah’s sons are listed again, now with her full lineage: “the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon.” Her ancestry is spelled out because she came from the native nobility of Seir (vv. 24-25). Her marriage joined Esau’s house to the Horite ruling families and gave her sons a strong claim in the land.

Unlike Adah and Bashemath, whose grandsons headed the clans, Aholibamah’s own three sons, Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah, became chiefs (v. 18). The phrase “she bare to Esau” underlines that they were Esau’s sons, a generation older than the other clan founders.

wordNotes.explanation: Bat normally means “daughter,” but it can also describe a granddaughter or any female descendant. Aholibamah is the daughter of Anah, and the following “daughter of Zibeon” traces her line back another generation. Rebekah, Nahor’s granddaughter, is likewise called the daughter of Abraham’s brother, and Jesus called a crippled woman “a daughter of Abraham.”

verses.bibleText: These were dukes of the sons of Esau: the sons of Eliphaz the firstborn son of Esau; duke Teman, duke Omar, duke Zepho, duke Kenaz,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“These were dukes of the sons of Esau” moves from family to government. The KJV’s “duke” comes from the Latin dux, “leader,” and renders the Hebrew ʾalluf, a tribal chief. The word may be linked with ʾelef, “thousand,” a term also used for a clan or military unit, so an ʾalluf was the head of such a group. Edom was organized as a confederation of clans under these leaders.

Eliphaz, “the firstborn son of Esau,” supplies the first chiefs: Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Kenaz, with three more in the next verse. Gatam, the fourth son in verse 11, is listed after Kenaz and Korah here, and the order of the two lists need not match.

These chiefs reappear in Israel’s song at the Red Sea: “Then the dukes of Edom shall be amazed” (Exodus 15:15). The leaders of Esau’s clans heard what God had done for Jacob’s descendants. Zechariah later uses the same word for the leaders of Judah strengthened by the LORD in the messianic age (Zechariah 12:5-6), and he pictures a converted remnant of the Philistines becoming “as a governor in Judah” (Zechariah 9:7). Leadership among the nations, too, comes under God’s saving rule.

wordNotes.explanation: The word means a chief or clan leader. Most occurrences describe the leaders of Edom and the Horites, though Exodus applies it to Edom’s chiefs trembling at the exodus, and Zechariah uses it for the governors of Judah. A related form describes a close friend or companion, as in “a whisperer separateth chief friends.”

verses.bibleText: Duke Korah, duke Gatam, and duke Amalek: these are the dukes that came of Eliphaz in the land of Edom; these were the sons of Adah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The list of Eliphaz’s chiefs continues with Korah, Gatam, and Amalek. Korah is unexpected here. He was named in verse 14 as a son of Aholibamah and is named again among her chiefs in verse 18, but he does not appear among Eliphaz’s sons in verse 11 or in 1 Chronicles 1:36. Either a copyist repeated the name from the nearby list, or a second Korah descended from Eliphaz led a clan of his own. The Samaritan text of the Pentateuch omits the name here.

Amalek, though the son of a concubine, is counted among the chiefs. This is the first use of “the land of Edom” in the chapter; the clans now possess territory, and the family has become a people with a homeland.

wordNotes.term: אֶרֶץ אֱדוֹם (ʾerets ʾEdom) — the land of Edom
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase names Esau’s territory after the man himself. Jacob had already sent messengers to “the land of Seir, the country of Edom.” Israel later camped “by the coast of the land of Edom” at mount Hor and had to travel around it when Edom refused passage.

verses.bibleText: And these are the sons of Reuel Esau's son; duke Nahath, duke Zerah, duke Shammah, duke Mizzah: these are the dukes that came of Reuel in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Bashemath Esau's wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Reuel’s four sons are now listed as chiefs: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. The closing words repeat that they came “of Reuel in the land of Edom” and were “the sons of Bashemath Esau’s wife.” Such repetition is typical of formal registers, where each entry is confirmed by its line of descent, as in Israel’s own census lists.

The careful record shows that the clans of Edom traced their authority back to Esau through particular mothers and sons. Israel’s tribes would be numbered in the same way, “by their families, by the house of their fathers” (Numbers 1:2).

wordNotes.explanation: The name may mean “he has heard” or be a shortened form of a longer name. It sounds the same as the noun shammah, “desolation” or “astonishment,” which Jeremiah later uses of Edom: “Edom shall be a desolation.” The resemblance is a sound play only and does not define the name’s meaning.

verses.bibleText: And these are the sons of Aholibamah Esau's wife; duke Jeush, duke Jaalam, duke Korah: these were the dukes that came of Aholibamah the daughter of Anah, Esau's wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Aholibamah’s sons, Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah, close the list of chiefs. The verse again names her as “the daughter of Anah,” keeping her Horite descent in view. She is the only one of Esau’s wives whose own sons, and not her grandsons, led clans.

Her name later appears as one of the chiefs of Edom listed by their places (v. 41), suggesting that a district or clan came to bear it. A woman from the native nobility thus left her name on the map of Edom.

wordNotes.explanation: The name may be connected with yaʿel, the wild mountain goat that leaps among the high rocks. Such goats were at home in rugged terrain like Seir and En-gedi. If the link is correct, the name suits the cliffs of the country where Esau’s clans settled.

verses.bibleText: These are the sons of Esau, who is Edom, and these are their dukes.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“These are the sons of Esau, who is Edom, and these are their dukes” sums up the section. It joins the family tree (vv. 10-14) to the political structure (vv. 15-18): the same men are both descendants and rulers. The refrain “who is Edom” sounds for the third time.

Within three generations Esau’s family had become a confederation of thirteen chiefs ruling a land of its own. Jacob’s twelve sons, by contrast, were still shepherds who would soon go down to Egypt, where shepherds were “an abomination” (46:34). Israel’s growth into a nation would come later, under affliction (Exodus 1:7, 12). Edom rose first, yet the promise had been that “the elder shall serve the younger” (25:23).

wordNotes.term: הוּא אֱדוֹם (hu ʾEdom) — who is Edom
wordNotes.explanation: The short clause, literally “he is Edom,” works as a refrain in this chapter. It reminds readers that the nation’s history grew from the choices of one man, the brother who sold his birthright for red stew. The Chronicler’s parallel list ends simply, “These are the dukes of Edom.”

verses.bibleText: These are the sons of Seir the Horite, who inhabited the land; Lotan, and Shobal, and Zibeon, and Anah,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter now turns to the people who held Seir before Esau: “the sons of Seir the Horite, who inhabited the land.” They first appear in Abraham’s day, when the eastern kings struck “the Horites in their mount Seir” (14:6). Seir here is a person, the ancestor of the clans, as well as the name of the region.

The Horites have often been identified with the Hurrians, a people widespread across Mesopotamia, Syria, and Anatolia in the second millennium before Christ and known from Egyptian and Hittite texts. An older view derived the name from ḥor, “hole” or “cave,” and pictured them as cave dwellers. The names in this list are mostly Semitic, so the Horites of Seir may have been a local group bearing a name that later also covered wider populations.

Deuteronomy explains what became of them: “the children of Esau succeeded them, when they had destroyed them from before them,” and it compares this with Israel’s own entry into Canaan (Deuteronomy 2:12, 22). God gave Esau his land much as he would give Israel theirs. The first four sons of Seir are Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, and Anah. Shobal is also the name of a Judahite clan founder associated with Kirjath-jearim (1 Chronicles 2:50), one of several overlaps between Seir’s families and Judah’s.

wordNotes.explanation: The singular form is used collectively for the whole people. Scripture places the Horites in mount Seir and records that God destroyed them before the children of Esau, who “dwelt in their stead.” The same form appears as a personal name (Hori) in verse 22, as though the people and an ancestor shared a name.

verses.bibleText: And Dishon, and Ezer, and Dishan: these are the dukes of the Horites, the children of Seir in the land of Edom.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan complete the seven sons of Seir. All seven are called “dukes of the Horites,” using the same title as Esau’s chiefs (v. 15). The Horites were already organized by clans under tribal leaders, and Esau’s family seems to have adopted or merged into that structure.

The phrase “in the land of Edom” uses the later name of the territory, written from the vantage point of a time when Esau’s descendants held it. Dishon and Dishan are nearly identical names, and Ezer was common enough to recur in Judah and in Nehemiah’s Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 4:4; Nehemiah 3:19).

wordNotes.explanation: The same word names one of the clean wild animals Israel was permitted to eat, rendered “pygarg” in the KJV and probably a kind of antelope or ibex. Animal names were common in the ancient world; Rachel means “ewe” and Deborah “bee.” The name links the Horite clan with the wildlife of its rugged homeland.

verses.bibleText: And the children of Lotan were Hori and Hemam; and Lotan's sister was Timna.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Lotan, the firstborn of Seir, had two sons, Hori and Hemam (spelled Homam in 1 Chronicles 1:39). The note “and Lotan’s sister was Timna” explains verse 12: the concubine of Eliphaz came from the leading Horite family. Women are seldom named in these lists unless they connect one line to another, and Timna is the link between the households of Esau and Seir.

The name Hori matches the name of the people, and it reappears in Israel’s history: Shaphat the son of Hori was the spy chosen from the tribe of Simeon (Numbers 13:5).

wordNotes.explanation: Timna is named as Lotan’s sister and as Eliphaz’s concubine, and the name later belongs to one of the chiefs of Edom listed by place (v. 40). A copper-mining valley in the southern Arabah still bears a similar name. The repetition shows a woman’s name becoming attached to a clan or district.

verses.bibleText: And the children of Shobal were these; Alvan, and Manahath, and Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Shobal had five sons: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. The Chronicler spells two of them slightly differently, Alian and Shephi (1 Chronicles 1:40). In Hebrew script the letters for w and y look much alike, which accounts for such small variations.

Several of these names surface later in Judah. Shobal the father of Kirjath-jearim had descendants called “half of the Manahethites” (1 Chronicles 2:52), and Onam occurs among the clans of Jerahmeel (1 Chronicles 2:26). Together with Kenaz (v. 11), these echoes suggest that families from Seir were absorbed into Judah. Ebal shares a name with one of Joktan’s sons (1 Chronicles 1:22); the mountain of that name in Ephraim has no evident connection with this clan.

wordNotes.explanation: The name is related to nuaḥ, “to rest,” and may mean “resting place.” The Manahethites appear among the descendants of Shobal and Salma in Judah’s genealogy, and a town called Manahath received exiled Benjamites. The name may have moved with a clan from Seir into the hill country of Judah.

verses.bibleText: And these are the children of Zibeon; both Ajah, and Anah: this was that Anah that found the mules in the wilderness, as he fed the asses of Zibeon his father.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Zibeon’s sons were Ajah and Anah, and the list pauses for its only story: “this was that Anah that found the mules in the wilderness, as he fed the asses of Zibeon his father.” The note distinguishes this Anah, Zibeon’s son and the father of Esau’s wife Aholibamah (vv. 2, 14), from Anah the son of Seir (v. 20). Moses refers to the event as something his readers already knew.

The Hebrew word rendered “mules,” yemim, occurs only here, and its meaning is uncertain. The KJV follows an old Jewish tradition that Anah first bred mules by crossing horses and donkeys. The Latin translation reads “hot springs,” and there are hot springs in the ravines east of the Dead Sea, in the very region where these clans lived. In a dry land, finding water while herding was worth remembering, much as Isaac’s servants celebrated “a well of springing water” in the valley of Gerar (26:19).

The scene of a son tending his father’s donkeys recalls Saul, who went looking for his father’s asses and found a kingdom (1 Samuel 9:3, 20). Ordinary work became the setting for a discovery remembered for generations. Ajah’s name is the word for a bird of prey listed among the unclean birds in the law (Leviticus 11:14).

wordNotes.explanation: This rare word has been interpreted as mules, as hot springs, or as waters. Because the law later forbade Israel to crossbreed animals, Israel probably obtained its mules by trade, and the first breeding of them would have been a memorable feat. The ancient translations divide on the meaning, and no other text settles it.

The name matches the word for a bird of prey, rendered “kite” in Leviticus and “vulture” in Job, known for its keen sight. The law lists it among the unclean birds, part of the distinction between clean and unclean creatures. Other people in Israel bore the name as well, including the father of Saul’s concubine Rizpah.

verses.bibleText: And the children of Anah were these; Dishon, and Aholibamah the daughter of Anah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Anah’s children were Dishon and Aholibamah. Following directly after the story of Zibeon’s son Anah, this verse identifies Esau’s wife (vv. 2, 14) as a granddaughter of Zibeon and great-granddaughter of Seir. Her place in the list explains her prominence among Esau’s wives and why her sons were counted as chiefs in their own right.

This Dishon, Anah’s son, should be distinguished from Dishon the son of Seir (v. 21). Names often recurred within a family across generations.

wordNotes.explanation: The phrase follows Aholibamah wherever she is named in the chapter, and here it finally connects her to the Horite family tree. The genealogy names a daughter only when she ties lines together, as when Genesis names Rebekah among Nahor’s descendants before she becomes Isaac’s wife.

verses.bibleText: And these are the children of Dishon; Hemdan, and Eshban, and Ithran, and Cheran.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Dishon’s four sons were Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran. These are the sons of Dishon the son of Seir, since verses 22-28 follow the order of Seir’s sons in verses 20-21. Chronicles reads Amram (or Hamran) for Hemdan, the Hebrew letters for d and r being easily confused (1 Chronicles 1:41).

Ithran recurs among the descendants of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:37). The others are known only from this list, but their preservation shows the care with which these neighboring families were recorded.

wordNotes.explanation: The name comes from ḥamad, “to desire” or “take delight in,” and probably means “pleasant” or “desirable.” The same verb describes the trees of Eden as “pleasant to the sight” and stands in the tenth commandment, “Thou shalt not covet.” In a personal name it expresses delight in a child and carries no moral weight.

verses.bibleText: The children of Ezer are these; Bilhan, and Zaavan, and Akan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Ezer’s sons were Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. Bilhan was also the name of a Benjamite (1 Chronicles 7:10). Akan appears as Jakan in 1 Chronicles 1:42, and that longer form connects with Bene-jaakan, “the children of Jaakan,” one of Israel’s camping places in the wilderness near Edom (Numbers 33:31-32).

Deuteronomy names “Beeroth of the children of Jaakan,” the wells of Jaakan’s clan, on Israel’s route (Deuteronomy 10:6). If the connection holds, Israel drew water from wells that carried the name of a Horite family descended from Seir.

wordNotes.explanation: The name appears as Jakan in Chronicles, and the clan seems to have given its name to Bene-jaakan and Beeroth Bene-jaakan, stations in Israel’s wilderness journey near mount Hor. The connection places this Horite family on the route Israel later traveled.

verses.bibleText: The children of Dishan are these; Uz, and Aran.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Dishan’s sons were Uz and Aran. Uz is a name with several bearers: a son of Aram (10:23) and Nahor’s firstborn, Huz (22:21). The most famous use is “the land of Uz,” where Job lived (Job 1:1). Lamentations places Uz beside Edom: “O daughter of Edom, that dwellest in the land of Uz” (Lamentations 4:21).

That link, together with Eliphaz the Temanite (v. 11), suggests that the book of Job is set among these very peoples. God called Job “a perfect and an upright man” (Job 1:8), a man of faith living outside Israel. The line of promise ran through Jacob, yet God was known and worshiped beyond it. Aran is otherwise unknown.

wordNotes.explanation: Uz names both persons and a region. Jeremiah lists “all the kings of the land of Uz” among nations made to drink the cup of God’s wrath, and Lamentations connects the land with Edom. The Horite clan named here is one likely source of the regional name.

verses.bibleText: These are the dukes that came of the Horites; duke Lotan, duke Shobal, duke Zibeon, duke Anah,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“These are the dukes that came of the Horites” begins a restatement of Seir’s seven sons as chiefs: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, and Anah, with the last three in the next verse. The pattern is the same as in Esau’s family: first the sons (vv. 20-28), then the chiefs (vv. 29-30). Genealogy and government are set side by side.

The parallel arrangement places the two peoples on equal footing. Before Esau’s descendants displaced them, the Horites were an organized society with recognized leaders.

wordNotes.term: אַלּוּפֵי הַחֹרִי (ʾallufe haḥori) — the dukes that came of the Horites
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the chiefs of the Horite,” using the collective singular for the people. The title is the same one given to Esau’s descendants, showing that Horites and Edomites shared a clan-based form of leadership in Seir.

verses.bibleText: Duke Dishon, duke Ezer, duke Dishan: these are the dukes that came of Hori, among their dukes in the land of Seir.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan complete the list of Horite chiefs. “These are the dukes that came of Hori, among their dukes in the land of Seir” closes the section. The KJV’s “of Hori” renders the same collective word translated “Horites” in the previous verse, and “among their dukes” means that each chief ruled his own clan.

The territory is called “the land of Seir” here and “the land of Edom” in verse 21. It was named first for the Horite ancestor and then for Esau. Deuteronomy says the children of Esau “dwelt in their stead, even unto this day” (Deuteronomy 2:22); the Horite record that ends here describes a people who were later replaced.

wordNotes.explanation: The phrase means “according to their chiefs” or “chief by chief,” presenting the Horites as a confederation of clans, each under its own head. A similar distributive phrase appears in the closing summary of Edom’s chiefs “according to their families.”

verses.bibleText: And these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel” introduces a list of eight rulers (vv. 32-39). The list has unusual features. No king is succeeded by his son, and each is linked with a different father, hometown, or district. Kingship in early Edom seems to have passed by choice or by the strength of a leading clan, rather like the judges who arose in Israel from different tribes. The Hebrew melekh covers a wide range of rulers: the five “kings of Midian” slain in Moses’ day (Numbers 31:8) are called “princes of Midian” elsewhere (Joshua 13:21). Edom’s kings need not have ruled a centralized state.

The clause about Israel is often taken to mean that the writer lived after Saul or David, and the Chronicler repeats it (1 Chronicles 1:43). That conclusion does not follow. God had promised Abraham that “kings shall come out of thee” (17:6, 16), and he had just renewed that promise to Jacob: “kings shall come out of thy loins” (35:11). Moses wrote with that promise before him. He gave laws for the day when Israel would set a king over itself (Deuteronomy 17:14-15), and he recorded Balaam’s oracle of a Sceptre rising out of Israel to possess Edom (Numbers 24:17-18). For a writer who knew Israel was destined to have kings, noting that Edom’s kings came first was natural. It measured Esau’s head start against a promise not yet fulfilled.

Moses also had firsthand knowledge of Edom’s monarchy. He sent messengers “unto the king of Edom” asking passage for Israel (Numbers 20:14), while the song at the Red Sea still speaks of Edom’s “dukes” (Exodus 15:15), so chiefs and kings coexisted. Eight reigns between the generation of Esau’s grandsons and Moses’ day span more than two centuries, a reasonable average for each king. The last king, Hadar, is the only one whose death is not reported (v. 39), whereas the Chronicler, writing much later, adds “Hadad died also” (1 Chronicles 1:51). That detail fits a writer for whom Hadar was still alive.

The verse also carries a lesson about timing. Worldly power came quickly to Esau; Israel would wait in Egypt and the wilderness for centuries before it had a king. When kingship came, David subdued Edom and “all they of Edom became David’s servants” (2 Samuel 8:14), so “the elder shall serve the younger” was fulfilled (25:23). The promise of kings to Jacob reached its height in David’s greater Son, who will reign as “King of kings, and Lord of lords” (Revelation 19:16).

wordNotes.term: לִפְנֵי מְלָךְ־מֶלֶךְ לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (lifne melokh-melekh livne Yisraʾel) — before there reigned any king over the children of Israel
wordNotes.explanation: The preposition lifne, “before,” sets a time frame. The clause can be read as “before an Israelite king reigned” or “before a king of Israel ruled over Edom”; the Greek translation reads “in Israel.” On either reading the comparison assumes a promised future in which Israel would have kings, a future God had already announced to the patriarchs and Moses had anticipated in the law.

The word can denote a great emperor, the ruler of a single city, or the head of a tribal people. Genesis already uses it for the petty kings of the cities of the plain. The rulers of Midian are called both kings and princes, showing how flexible the title was in Moses’ time.

verses.bibleText: And Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom: and the name of his city was Dinhabah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The first king, Bela the son of Beor, ruled from Dinhabah, a town that has not been located. The phrase “the name of his city was” recurs for three kings (vv. 32, 35, 39), indicating that each ruled from his own base and that the seat of power moved with the king.

The name “son of Beor” recalls Balaam the son of Beor, the diviner hired by Moab to curse Israel (Numbers 22:5), and some ancient readers connected the two. Balaam, however, came from Pethor near the Euphrates and lived in Moses’ day, generations after Edom’s first king. Bela was also the name of Benjamin’s firstborn (46:21) and the older name of Zoar (14:2).

wordNotes.term: בֶּלַע בֶּן־בְּעוֹר (Belaʿ ben-Beʿor) — Bela the son of Beor
wordNotes.explanation: Bela may come from a root meaning “to swallow.” The same name belongs to Benjamin’s eldest son and to the city later called Zoar, and the patronymic matches that of Balaam. Such shared names were common in the region and do not by themselves identify persons.

verses.bibleText: And Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his stead.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Bela was followed by “Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah.” His father may have belonged to the clan of Zerah, Reuel’s son (v. 13). Bozrah, identified with modern Buseirah south-southeast of the Dead Sea, became Edom’s chief city, a fortress overlooking the King’s Highway. An old tradition attached to the Greek version of Job identified Job with this Jobab, but Scripture makes no such connection.

Bozrah became a byword in the prophets for Edom itself. Amos announced fire that would “devour the palaces of Bozrah” (Amos 1:12), Jeremiah foretold that “Bozrah shall become a desolation” (Jeremiah 49:13), and Isaiah spoke of “a sacrifice in Bozrah” (Isaiah 34:6).

Isaiah’s most striking image asks, “Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” The answer is the LORD himself, who has “trodden the winepress alone” to bring judgment and redemption (Isaiah 63:1-4). Revelation takes up that picture for Christ, clothed “with a vesture dipped in blood,” who “treadeth the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God” (Revelation 19:13-15). The town of an early Edomite king became the setting for a prophecy of the Redeemer’s final victory over every enemy of his people.

wordNotes.explanation: The name is related to batsar, a verb used for fortifying a city and, in a separate sense, for gathering grapes. The first sense suits a stronghold, and Isaiah’s picture of garments stained as in a winepress may play on the second. Micah also mentions “the sheep of Bozrah,” though that may refer to a fold or to a different town.

verses.bibleText: And Jobab died, and Husham of the land of Temani reigned in his stead.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The third king, Husham, came “of the land of Temani,” the district named after Teman, Eliphaz’s eldest son (v. 11). In a few generations the clan had become a recognized region. The kings came from different parts of Edom in turn: Dinhabah, Bozrah, and now Teman.

Teman was known for its wise men. Obadiah asked whether the LORD would not “destroy the wise men out of Edom” and dismay the “mighty men, O Teman” (Obadiah 1:8-9). The wisdom of Teman, represented by Job’s friend, would not save Edom from judgment.

wordNotes.term: אֶרֶץ הַתֵּימָנִי (ʾerets hattemani) — the land of Temani
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the land of the Temanite,” using the gentilic form that also describes Job’s friend Eliphaz. The phrase shows a clan name becoming a regional name within Edom, one that the prophets used in parallel with Edom as a whole.

verses.bibleText: And Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who smote Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his stead: and the name of his city was Avith.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hadad the son of Bedad is the only king remembered for a deed: he “smote Midian in the field of Moab.” Midian’s tribes, descended from Abraham and Keturah (25:2), ranged widely through the desert. Later Moab and Midian joined forces against Israel and hired Balaam together (Numbers 22:4, 7), so alliances among these peoples shifted over time. Hadad ruled from Avith, which has not been identified.

Hadad was the name of the storm god of Syria, often identified with Baal, and royal names honoring him continued in Edom; a later Hadad of the royal house fled to Egypt and troubled Solomon (1 Kings 11:14-22). Midian, too, would trouble Israel until God broke its power through Gideon, a victory Isaiah recalled when promising deliverance through the coming Child: “as in the day of Midian” (Isaiah 9:4-6).

wordNotes.term: שְׂדֵה מוֹאָב (sedeh Moʾav) — the field of Moab
wordNotes.explanation: Sadeh can mean a field or open country, and here it describes Moab’s plateau land north of Edom. Naomi’s family went to sojourn in “the country of Moab,” using the same expression, and Genesis earlier speaks of “the country of Edom” in the same way.

Hadad was the name of the West Semitic storm god, and it appears in royal names such as Ben-hadad of Damascus and in the place name Hadadrimmon. Edom’s use of it shows that its rulers honored the gods of the surrounding peoples.

verses.bibleText: And Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his stead.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Samlah of Masrekah succeeded Hadad. His name resembles simlah, the ordinary word for a cloak or outer garment, and Masrekah may mean “vineyard place,” from a word for choice vines. A site south of Maʿan in southern Jordan has been suggested, but the location is uncertain.

Like Jobab and Husham, Samlah is identified by his town, not his father. Kingship moved again to a new district.

wordNotes.explanation: The name may be related to soreq, a choice red vine. Jacob’s blessing of Judah speaks of binding “his ass’s colt unto the choice vine,” and Isaiah’s vineyard song says God planted Israel “with the choicest vine.” If the connection holds, Masrekah was a vine-growing settlement.

verses.bibleText: And Samlah died, and Saul of Rehoboth by the river reigned in his stead.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The sixth king, “Saul of Rehoboth by the river,” bears the same name as Israel’s first king. Shaul means “asked,” and Israel would one day ask for a king “to judge us like all the nations” (1 Samuel 8:5). Edom had its Saul centuries earlier.

Rehoboth means “broad places,” the name Isaac gave to the well where at last there was no strife: “now the LORD hath made room for us” (26:22). “The river” usually means the Euphrates in Scripture, but an Edomite king is more likely to have come from a town on a local stream, perhaps near the Zered on Edom’s northern border.

wordNotes.explanation: The name is the passive participle of shaʾal, “to ask,” meaning “asked for.” It was borne by a son of Simeon, by Israel’s first king, and later by Saul of Tarsus. Samuel’s narrative plays on the name when the people ask for a king and receive Saul.

wordNotes.term: רְחֹבוֹת הַנָּהָר (Reḥovot hannahar) — Rehoboth by the river
wordNotes.explanation: Reḥovot means “wide places” or “room.” The same name was given to Isaac’s well and is part of a city name in Assyria. The qualifying phrase distinguishes this town, but the river intended is unclear.

verses.bibleText: And Saul died, and Baal-hanan the son of Achbor reigned in his stead.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Baal-hanan the son of Achbor is the only king of the list given neither a city nor a town of origin. His name means “Baal is gracious,” confessing the god of the land in the same pattern by which Israelite names such as Johanan and Hananiah confess that the LORD is gracious (Exodus 34:6).

The same name was later borne by David’s overseer of olive and sycamore trees (1 Chronicles 27:28). Achbor recurs as the name of an official in Josiah’s court (2 Kings 22:12).

wordNotes.explanation: The name joins Baʿal, “lord” or the god Baal, with ḥanan, “he has been gracious.” Israel confessed the same quality of the LORD, who proclaimed himself “merciful and gracious.” The contrast between the two names shows which god each people credited with grace.

The name resembles ʿakhbar, “mouse,” which the law lists among the unclean creeping things. Animal names were common and carried no stigma; an Achbor later served Josiah, and his son Elnathan was a prince in Jeremiah’s day.

verses.bibleText: And Baal-hanan the son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his stead: and the name of his city was Pau; and his wife's name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hadar, the eighth king, breaks the pattern. The text records his city, Pau, and gives his wife’s name, Mehetabel, with her mother and grandmother, Matred and Mezahab. It does not say that he died. Chronicles calls him Hadad, spells his city Pai, and adds, “Hadad died also” (1 Chronicles 1:50-51); the Chronicler wrote long after this king’s reign ended.

The silence about Hadar’s death and the personal detail about his household suggest that he was reigning when Genesis was written. He may be the king of Edom to whom Moses sent the message, “Thus saith thy brother Israel,” asking only to pass along the king’s highway. Edom refused and came out “with much people, and with a strong hand,” and Israel turned away (Numbers 20:14-21).

Israel did not fight, because God had said, “Meddle not with them” (Deuteronomy 2:4-5). Moses honored the brotherhood even when it was not returned. Mehetabel means “God does good,” and the name of Hadar’s queen bears unintended witness to the goodness of the God who had given Esau his land.

wordNotes.explanation: The name means “God does good” or “God benefits,” from the verb yatav, “to be good” or “do good.” Jacob reminded God of his promise, “I will surely do thee good,” and the psalmist confessed, “Thou art good, and doest good.” A man named Mehetabeel appears in Nehemiah’s day.

The name means “waters of gold.” It may be a personal name or a place name describing the family’s origin. A similar place name, Dizahab, “abundance of gold,” appears in the opening verse of Deuteronomy.

verses.bibleText: And these are the names of the dukes that came of Esau, according to their families, after their places, by their names; duke Timnah, duke Alvah, duke Jetheth,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The final list names “the dukes that came of Esau, according to their families, after their places, by their names.” The arrangement is geographic as well as genealogical. Several names already appeared as persons: Timnah recalls Timna (vv. 12, 22), and Aholibamah, Kenaz, and Teman follow in the next verses. Here they seem to designate clans and the districts those clans occupied, perhaps the administrative regions of Edom in the time of its last king.

The formula echoes the table of nations, where the sons of Shem are listed “after their families, after their tongues, in their lands, after their nations” (10:31). Esau’s descendants are treated as one of the peoples of the earth, with families and territories of their own. Timnah, Alvah, and Jetheth begin the list; Alvah may be the clan of Alvan (v. 23), and Jetheth is otherwise unknown.

wordNotes.term: לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָם לִמְקֹמֹתָם בִּשְׁמֹתָם (lemishpeḥotam limqomotam bishmotam) — according to their families, after their places, by their names
wordNotes.explanation: Three parallel phrases sort the chiefs by clan, location, and name. The pattern recalls the closing formulas of the table of nations, which group the descendants of Japheth, Ham, and Shem by families and lands. Edom is presented as a nation with recognized territories.

verses.bibleText: Duke Aholibamah, duke Elah, duke Pinon,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Aholibamah, Elah, and Pinon continue the list. Aholibamah, the name of Esau’s Horite wife (v. 2), now marks a clan or district. Elah is probably Elath, the port at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, which Israel passed on the way around Edom (Deuteronomy 2:8). Solomon later built ships at Ezion-geber “beside Eloth” (1 Kings 9:26), and the town changed hands between Judah and Edom more than once (2 Kings 14:22; 16:6).

Pinon is Punon, one of Israel’s wilderness camps (Numbers 33:42-43), in the copper-rich district east of the Arabah, where ancient mines and smelting sites have been found. Israel came through this region as it went “to compass the land of Edom,” and on that stage of the journey the fiery serpents struck the people and Moses lifted up a serpent of bronze (Numbers 21:4-9).

Jesus took that event as a picture of his own death: “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up” (John 3:14-15). A list of Edomite chiefs touches the place where Israel learned to look and live.

wordNotes.explanation: The name corresponds to Punon, a station of Israel’s journey after Zalmonah, in a region known for copper. The bronze serpent Moses made during the march around Edom was fashioned from that metal, and Jesus applied the lifted serpent to his cross.

The name means “terebinth” or “great tree,” and it is probably the same place as Elath or Eloth on the Gulf of Aqaba. Its harbor made it valuable to every power in the region, and Judah and Edom contested it for centuries.

verses.bibleText: Duke Kenaz, duke Teman, duke Mibzar,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Kenaz, Teman, and Mibzar follow. Kenaz and Teman were sons of Eliphaz (v. 11) and chiefs (v. 15); now they appear as districts, showing how clan names became regional names over time.

Mibzar means “fortress,” and it may refer to Bozrah or another stronghold. David’s psalm asks, “Who will bring me into the strong city? who will lead me into Edom?” and answers, “Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies” (Psalm 60:9, 12). Edom’s fortresses could not withstand the God who had given the land and who also governs its future.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun means a fortified place or stronghold. Reuben and Gad promised to leave their families in “fenced cities,” using this word, and David’s psalm calls Edom’s citadel ʿir mivtsar, “the strong city.” As a clan name it may preserve the memory of a fortress in Edom.

verses.bibleText: Duke Magdiel, duke Iram: these be the dukes of Edom, according to their habitations in the land of their possession: he is Esau the father of the Edomites.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Magdiel and Iram complete the eleven chiefs. Magdiel may mean “gift of God” or “God is excellence,” from meged, the word for choice produce in Moses’ blessing of Joseph (Deuteronomy 33:13-16). Iram is otherwise unknown. Then comes the summary: “these be the dukes of Edom, according to their habitations in the land of their possession: he is Esau the father of the Edomites.”

“The land of their possession” is a weighty phrase. The word ʾaḥuzzah is the one God used when he promised Abraham “all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession” (17:8), and it describes the cave of Machpelah, the only piece of Canaan the patriarchs owned (23:20). When this chapter closes, Edom already holds its possession, while Jacob owns a grave and a promise. The next verse makes the contrast explicit: “Jacob dwelt in the land wherein his father was a stranger” (37:1). Edom’s land was a true gift from God (Deuteronomy 2:5), but it was a portion in this age only.

“He is Esau the father of the Edomites” closes the chapter as it began. Genesis records the deaths of Abraham, Isaac, and later Jacob, but it never reports Esau’s. His story ends absorbed into the nation that bears his name. The prophets later announced that Edom’s pride would be brought low (Obadiah 1:3-4; Malachi 1:2-4), and history bore it out: the Edomites were driven from Seir and later absorbed into Judea, disappearing as a people. When Paul quotes Malachi, “Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated” (Romans 9:13), he speaks of God’s free choice of the line that would bring the Messiah, not of a decree barring any Edomite from mercy.

The door remained open. The law said, “Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother,” and allowed his children to enter the congregation of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:7-8). Crowds from Idumea came to hear Jesus (Mark 3:8). Believers in Christ are promised “an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away” (1 Peter 1:4). That inheritance is open to Jacob’s children and Esau’s alike, through faith in the Seed of Abraham.

wordNotes.term: אֶרֶץ אֲחֻזָּתָם (ʾerets ʾaḥuzzatam) — the land of their possession
wordNotes.explanation: ʾAḥuzzah, from ʾaḥaz, “to grasp” or “take hold,” denotes property held as one’s own. God promised Canaan to Abraham’s seed as an “everlasting possession,” and the same term is used for the burial cave Abraham bought, the only land the patriarchs owned. Jacob repeated the promise to Joseph on his deathbed. In this chapter Edom already holds what Israel is still waiting to receive.

The name probably joins meged, “choice thing” or “precious gift,” with ʾEl, “God.” Meged describes the precious fruits of heaven and earth in Moses’ blessing of Joseph and the “pleasant fruits” of the garden in the Song of Solomon.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: Why would Scripture give a whole chapter to the family of the brother who sold his birthright?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God kept his word to Esau and made him a nation with chiefs and kings, yet the inheritance of promise stayed with Jacob, who waited by faith in a land he did not yet own.
discussionQuestions: What does the careful record of Esau’s descendants reveal about God’s attitude toward people outside the line of promise?
How does Esau’s move away from Canaan compare with Lot’s choice in Genesis 13?
Why might Israel in the wilderness have been tempted to envy Edom, and what does Genesis 37:1 teach about waiting?
How could Moses write of kings in Edom “before there reigned any king over the children of Israel”?
How do Amos 9:12 and Acts 15:16-17 change the way we read the long story of Edom?
commonMisunderstandings: Verse 31 does not require a writer living after Saul; Moses knew God had promised kings to Jacob (35:11) and had himself dealt with a king of Edom.
The differences between the wives’ names here and in chapters 26 and 28 reflect the ancient use of more than one name, not conflicting records.
God’s choice of Jacob concerned the line through which the promised Seed would come; it never shut Edomites out of grace (Deuteronomy 23:7-8).
Edom’s quick rise to kingship is no sign of greater favor; worldly power often matures faster than the promises of God.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Read the lists as evidence of God’s reliability: every name shows a promise to Esau kept, and that reliability guarantees the greater promises carried by Jacob’s line to Christ.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Do not trade the birthright for what can be held today; rest your hope on the promises of God fulfilled in Jesus, and wait for the inheritance he has prepared.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God keeps every word he speaks, and the inheritance that lasts is received by faith in the promised Seed rather than gained through worldly success.
flow: God promised Rebekah two nations, and Genesis 36 shows Esau’s nation fully formed.
Esau gained wives, wealth, land, chiefs, and kings, yet he had despised the birthright that carried the promise.
Jacob stayed as a stranger in Canaan, trusting God for an inheritance he could not yet see.
Christ, the Seed of Jacob, opens that inheritance to everyone who believes, including the remnant of Edom.
Each hearer must choose between the portion this world offers now and the kingdom God gives by faith.
simpleIllustrations: A man sells a deed to a field for a meal because he is hungry tonight; years later he owns a busy shop, but the field held the treasure.
Two brothers leave a reading of a will; one takes the cash and moves away, the other stays on the land because he trusts what the will promises.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you choose the inheritance God promises in Christ over the success that can be grasped today?
cautions: Do not present Esau or the Edomites as beyond the reach of grace; Scripture foresees Edomites among the nations called by God’s name.
Do not read Romans 9 as teaching that individuals are born destined for destruction; it concerns God’s free choice of the line of promise.
Do not use the chapter to measure God’s blessing by wealth or political power.

reflectionQuestions: Am I tempted, like Esau, to value what I can hold now above what God has promised?
Do I recognize God’s goodness in the lives of people who do not share my faith?
When others prosper quickly while I wait on God, how do I respond?
What would it mean for me to live as a stranger and pilgrim, as Jacob did in Canaan?
Do I pray for people whose families have long been hostile to God, believing that Christ can gather them too?
